newsitem.title: USA: Scientists spot new planet orbiting Sun-like star.
newsitem.headline: Scientists spot new planet orbiting Sun-like star.

text.p: A new planet bigger than Jupiter has been spotted orbiting a Sun-like star trillions of miles (kilometers) from Earth, and the discovery could shake up ideas of how planetary systems form, according to a new report by astronomers.

The star, known as 16 Cygni B and located in the constellation Cygnus, or Northern Cross, is similar in mass and chemical composition to the Sun, according to researchers at the University of Texas and San Francisco State University.
They presented their findings in Tucson on Wednesday at a meeting of the Division of Planetary Sciences at the American Astronomical Society,

Observing 16 Cygni B over more than two years, the scientists found that its rotational velocity changed by about 100 miles (160.9 km) an hour, and they concluded from this that a large planet -- about 1.6 times the mass of Jupiter -- was orbiting the star at a distance of about 158 million miles (254.3 million km).
The researchers said the size and orbital distance of the new planet are similar to those of a planet recently reported to be circling the star 47 Ursae Majoris.
"It's exciting to find a planet orbiting a star that is nearly identical to the Sun," researcher William Cochran of the University of Texas said in a statement.

"But a year ago, we would have predicted that a planet around such a star would be pretty much like our solar system, with small, rocky planets close in and big, gaseous planets farther out," Cochran said. "Instead, we're finding that planetary systems are all different and this is one of the strangest yet."
